# Payroll onboarding and workforce administration

Checkpoint 501 (Maryland MW507 certificate groundwork): Retained the official 2026 two-page MW507 with SHA-256 f3a0ac6ac464042b8bbd63ee0d61cbdf464bea5f05124f731e660630caec6140. Added validated identity/rate/claim data, the personal-exemptions worksheet with AGI bands and downward truncation, and a PDF renderer preserving the original instructions, fields and worksheet. Claim types distinguish no-liability, reciprocal-state domicile, Pennsylvania state-only versus local exemptions, and military-spouse certification. Review metadata identifies more-than-ten exemptions, nonresidence/military submission reasons, additional-withholding agreement needs, no-liability weekly-wage review, renewal and military attachments. These are obligations, not evidence of agency acceptance. The original grouped checkbox fields require canonical value plus individual widget-state handling; normal checkbox selection would choose the wrong rate/domicile. Thirteen MW507/W-4 form and PDF regression checks passed (/tmp/payroll-mw507-renderer-regression.log); scoped lint passed. Three synthetic PDFs were reopened and all 32 canonical/widget pairs per PDF, read-only flags and appearance states verified. Ordinary pages 1–2, Pennsylvania and no-liability page 1 were rendered and inspected. The official nine-character SSN field retains normalized digits. Assumptions: preserve explicit claim basis; additional withholding does not itself create an employer agreement; attachments, revocation review and required Comptroller submissions must be completed separately before applicable automation. This is backend form groundwork only: employee screens, encrypted draft/signature transactions, admin election transfer, attachment workflow, submission/renewal tracking and production acceptance remain unfinished. No payroll election was changed or production filing made. The full onboarding goal remains active.

Checkpoint 500 (internal W-4 deductions worksheet): Added the page-4 2026 deductions worksheet to employee onboarding, with detailed single/separate/joint/surviving-spouse/head-of-household status matched to Step 1(c). The helper calculates qualified-estimate caps, senior amounts, medical/charity expense floors, state/local caps, itemized limitation, standard-deduction comparison and the final additional Step 4(b) amount. It does not enter the standard deduction itself as an additional deduction or count charitable gifts twice. Unsupported income/debt limitation cases stop with an explanation instead of silently omitting a claimed estimate; separate filers must confirm standard-deduction eligibility. Inputs are employee-provided eligible estimates; this is the printed annual worksheet, not a full eligibility/phaseout or tax-return engine. Applying explicitly replaces Step 4(b); changing worksheet inputs hides stale results. An unsigned text record is downloadable; raw estimates stay in memory and only the applied result follows encrypted draft/signature storage. Ten worksheet calculation tests passed (/tmp/payroll-w4-deductions-unit-final.log), including filing distinctions, caps, floors, limitation boundaries, the senior skip rule, equality selection, malformed input and integer overflow. Review caught and fixed a half-cent error: expense deductions now round after subtraction, with an explicit regression test. Both complete browser journeys passed (/tmp/payroll-w4-deductions-browser.log, 1.6 minutes), proving calculation/download, explicit application, stale-result handling, draft resume, signed PDF amount, signature retry and admin transfer of the $2,100 ordinary deduction; exempt fields stayed blank. Mobile result lines were visually inspected. Scoped lint, whitespace and final build passed (/tmp/payroll-w4-deductions-build-final.log), with existing warnings. Assumptions: blank optional estimates mean zero; employees review eligibility; dollar calculations use integer cents and round percentage results half up; detailed household estimates are not sent to admins. Sources: retained 2026 IRS Form W-4 page 4 and IRS Schedule 1-A for the stated married/SSN eligibility restrictions. Remaining: comprehensive eligibility/phaseout and year-to-date estimator, wider multiple-job cases, renewals/history, additional scripts/fonts, state/I-9 internal completion and broader onboarding/production requirements. No production action or public push occurred; the full goal remains active.

Checkpoint 499 (internal multiple-jobs W-4 worksheet): Added the printed 2026 Step 2(b) two-/three-job worksheet inside employee onboarding. Calculations sort annual taxable wages, perform both three-job lookups, show each worksheet line, use an explicitly entered highest-job annual pay frequency, round the final division to cents and add other requested per-check withholding. Explicit application requires confirmation that this is the highest-paying job, replaces Step 4(c), clears alternative Step 2(c), and invalidates stale calculation results when inputs change. Employees can download an unsigned text worksheet for their records; raw household wages remain in memory, while the applied result uses existing encrypted draft/signature storage. Four focused calculation checks passed, including all three filing tables, band/cents boundaries, the inclusive $120,000 limit, integer rounding and invalid inputs. Both ordinary/exempt browser journeys passed (55.2 seconds, /tmp/payroll-w4-worksheet-browser.log), including downloaded record contents and ordinary signing/admin transfer. A further ordinary browser check verified three-job results and encrypted draft resume of the applied amount (/tmp/payroll-w4-worksheet-resume-browser.log); the mobile worksheet screenshot was inspected. Scoped lint, table-source comparison, whitespace and final build passed (/tmp/payroll-w4-worksheet-build-final.log), with existing build warnings. Assumptions: annual taxable wages include concurrent spouse jobs for joint filers; no invented default pay frequency; no automatic transliteration or transmission of household wages; explicit replacement of the current extra withholding. Remaining: internal deductions worksheet, expanded tables for higher multiple-job wages/more jobs, year-to-date/partial-year estimator, renewals, state/I-9 native completion and broader production/onboarding requirements. No production action or public push occurred; the full goal remains active.

Checkpoint 496 (encrypted resumable W-4 drafts): Added employee-only draft read/save endpoints and checklist controls. Partial names, SSNs, choices and unfinished dollar entries are validated as draft data and encrypted with facility/employee/task/onboarding-cycle AAD; no signature can be saved in a draft. Drafts resume under a new authenticated session, use revision checks and exact retry keys to prevent stale overwrites, and return no-store responses. The UI saves explicitly, reloads saved work, retains no draft in browser storage and requires a fresh form preview/signature. Signing atomically clears encrypted draft content while advancing its retained revision and binding the new signed submission, preventing older tabs from resurrecting it. Scope/revision/session guards also protect database writes. The expanded browser journey passed (`/tmp/payroll-w4-draft-browser.log`), including saving a partial SSN, reload/resume, completed signature/retry and admin election transfer. Four serial draft/signature/native-election/workforce regression tests passed with no skips (`/tmp/payroll-w4-draft-regression.log`, 62.13 seconds). Additional draft access checks passed (`/tmp/payroll-w4-draft-scope.log`): foreign employee read/write denied, cross-facility row mutation denied and missing vault key returns 503. Scoped lint, whitespace and build passed (`/tmp/payroll-w4-draft-build.log`) with existing warnings. Assumptions: saving is explicit; drafts are unsigned and do not change elections; reloading deliberately replaces unsaved screen entries; only the current draft is retained, while signed forms retain their immutable history; a new session can resume a draft but requires a fresh signing preview. Remaining: exemption/nonresident/lock-in paths, automated worksheets, Unicode fonts, wider rehire/history and provider/production completion. No production migration/deployment or public push occurred; the original goal remains active.

Checkpoint 495 (signed W-4 to reviewed federal elections): Added a scoped vault reader that derives federal withholding choices from the latest signed W-4 for the current onboarding cycle. Admin pay setup prepopulates and locks the signed federal values, shows whether checklist review is complete, and sends the exact submission/fingerprint when saving state and federal elections. The server rejects unreviewed, changed, stale or missing native sources, altered federal values and an existing IRS lock-in restriction. Saved elections retain signed-document provenance. Generic task resubmission cannot erase an internal signature reference; amendments use the internal signing flow. Signing a new form marks the employee W-4 requested and existing elections pending review; onboarding readiness, the regular calculator and standalone PTO/bonus preparation reject using those pending settings until current elections are saved. The expanded browser journey passed (`/tmp/payroll-w4-admin-transfer-browser.log`): employee signs/retries, admin completes checklist review, federal fields are prepopulated/read-only, and save retains the exact signed amounts/source. Two focused DB tests passed, then 15 broader checks passed with no skips (`/tmp/payroll-w4-transfer-regression.log`, 81.08 seconds), including source mismatch/tampering, amendment invalidation, signature retention, withholding, standalone PTO/bonus and existing workforce/QuickBooks fixtures. Scoped ESLint, whitespace and build passed (`/tmp/payroll-w4-transfer-build.log`) with existing warnings. Assumptions: admin still verifies the actual form and state/local evidence; signed federal choices cannot be edited by an admin; an amendment prevents old settings from being reused while review is pending. Remaining: exempt forms correctly retain a blank filing status but the calculator still needs native exempt-path support, nonresident/lock-in handling, encrypted drafts, worksheet automation, Unicode fonts, wider amendment/date/history and production/provider completion. This proves the covered supported local workflow, not all-new-hire or production completion. No production migration/deployment or public push occurred.

Checkpoint 481 (effective agreement and committed-period loading): Added read-only effective-date agreement selection and period loading for a scoped employee. Period loading requires one complete payment-date period, reconciles actual APPROVED rows as reservations through a distinct validator (without inventing employee statements), and still requires finalized statement evidence for paid rows. It feeds the allocator scoped component evidence and source hashes, excludes VOID through status selection, and permits self-exclusion only for a scoped unfinalized run on the same payment date. An initial test used unsupported onboarding status PENDING and was corrected to REQUESTED. These loaders remain read-only and are not yet called by payroll calculation/approval/finalization to allocate deductions. Next: connect allocation to regular and PTO calculations together, retain partial/zero applied components, cover bonus and historical sources, verify employer-lock concurrency and imported-history completeness, and expose the applied/remaining amounts. No production actions occurred; the original goal remains active.

## Implemented flows

- Admin creates a hire and an employee-specific 13-step onboarding packet in one transaction.
- Invitation redemption opens an employee-only session. Employees can set a password for subsequent sign-in; a new invitation can recover access. Tokens are hashed and passwords use bcrypt.
- Employees submit personal/emergency contacts, signed tax/I-9 forms, payment election, wage-notice and handbook acknowledgments, and availability.
- PDF, PNG, and JPEG uploads are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, bound to facility, employee, and onboarding task. Document reads require scoped authentication and are audited. Uploads fail closed if the encryption key is absent.
- Admin reviews submissions and records evidence, requests corrections, records justified exceptions, verifies I-9/employment setup, and completes the first-shift checklist. Activation requires all mandatory steps to be resolved.
- Paid leave accepts explicit hours by date, routes those hours to the appropriate payroll periods, and debits the leave balance once per approved request.
- Employee leave, time-correction, availability, expense, and general requests have persistent approval history. Sick-leave approval debits the ledger exactly once. Time correction returns to timesheet review. Expense approval creates a one-period reimbursement after explicit tax-treatment confirmation.
- Admins can edit individual shifts as well as cancel them; concurrent edits and creation serialize per employee to protect overlap checks.
- Weekly recurring shifts preserve facility-local time across daylight-saving transitions. Shift creation detects overlaps and approved leave.
- Payroll prevents duplicate non-void runs per period, rejects stale calculations at approval, requires verified withholding, and records final payment confirmation. Finalized payroll creates employee statements and sick-leave accrual.
- Direct QuickBooks OAuth connection, real chart-of-accounts selection, immutable journal requests, idempotent retries, sync history, and optional automatic sync on finalization. CSV export remains available.
- Daily workforce automation initializes packets, prepares three months of semimonthly pay periods, flags due onboarding, pending requests, and long-open clocks, and retries enabled QuickBooks syncs.
- Finalized payroll freezes employer contact details and named pay items into the statement snapshot. Employees can download an itemized PDF and see withholding/deduction breakdowns in the portal. PDF layout and authenticated cross-employee access were verified.
- Former employees retain sign-in and record downloads; work/onboarding changes and new leave/availability requests are disabled.
- Native employer FUTA and Maryland UI calculations use verified effective/assigned rates and separate $7,000/$8,500 annual wage caps. Employer costs flow into payroll and QuickBooks; the tax-liability export itemizes them separately from employee withholding.
- Native 2026 federal withholding and Maryland 3.20% local semimonthly withholding use admin-verified signed-form elections. Unsupported elections remain blocked for separately verified withholding. Exempt claims do not bypass value validation.
- Missing-clock requests create exactly one attested time entry after admin review. Database guards reject overlapping time and changes to approved/finalized payroll. Open clocks block approval without crashing preview. Rejected entries are excluded. Overnight entries are segmented at facility-local midnight across pay periods and workweeks; ambiguous overnight unpaid breaks require corrected source entries.
- QuickBooks sandbox and production sync identities are distinct.
- Schema startup runs transactionally under a PostgreSQL advisory lock. Concurrent boot tests preserve employees and compensation.
- Startup no longer replays historical employer/employee/payment seed data that could overwrite pay rates or duplicate historical payments.

- Effective-dated hourly compensation preserves opening rates and applies future changes by facility-local workday. Admin records written notice, employee can acknowledge receipt, and PDFs/online statements itemize hours and wages at each rate. Onboarding rate edits reopen wage acknowledgment and admin pay review.
- PTO credits do not consume the Maryland sick-leave annual accrual cap; future-dated credits are excluded from the target payroll calculation.

- Payroll runs freeze a payment date independently of the scheduled payday. The date drives year-to-date wages, tax-year selection, statements, registers, sick accrual posting, and QuickBooks journals. Finalization requires a matching actual date and rejects future payments; it rechecks calculation inputs and blockers after approval. Earlier approved payments must be finalized before later payroll is approved.

- Internal tax reconciliation derives quarterly liabilities from finalized payment dates, tracks actual deposit receipts and void history, and compares accepted filing control totals with saved payroll snapshots. Later payroll changes and differing totals are flagged. Daily automation flags outstanding receipt balances and filing comparisons needing review.

- Each payroll workspace receives eight employer compliance reviews automatically on startup, first use, and daily maintenance. They do not depend on a particular employee. New workplaces start with blank employer identity; historical company identity is not copied during startup. Reviewed statuses and evidence survive restart; completing registration reviews updates Employer setup. Critical unfinished reviews block payroll approval and finalization.

- QuickBooks authorization links are single-use, bound to the initiating configuration and workplace, and invalidated by disconnect. Reconnecting the same company retains verified mappings; switching companies clears mapping and automatic sync. Connection, mapping, and disconnect changes are audited without token values.

## Assumptions to review

1. Vortex's operating baseline is a Maryland workplace, America/New_York timezone, hourly nonexempt employees, and a Monday workweek. Other worker/pay configurations need explicit supported calculation paths rather than silently using hourly Maryland rules.
2. The existing owner-selected semimonthly schedule (5th and 20th) remains the baseline. Paydays move earlier for weekends and standard Federal Reserve bank holidays. Bank/provider submission cutoff times remain separate; special local closures need operational review. Regeneration preserves dates attached to existing non-void payroll runs.
3. Signed W-4, state withholding, and I-9 documents may be uploaded internally or completed through a designated secure provider with an auditable receipt. A receipt is a submission, not automatic approval.
4. Employees may choose paper checks. Direct-deposit activation requires provider setup and admin verification; a checkbox does not initiate a bank transfer.
5. A hiring admin publishes the actual handbook, leave/benefit policies, and first-day instructions. The system does not invent an adopted company handbook.
6. Admin review is required for statutory forms, payment setup, classification/benefits, safeguarding/training, and new-hire reporting. Employee submissions never self-approve.
7. I-9 employer review due dates use three weekdays after hire; the admin must verify holidays, short-duration employment, and any applicable exceptions. State new-hire reporting starts with a 20-calendar-day reminder and requires jurisdiction-specific confirmation.
8. Sick leave initially uses the existing Maryland accrual ledger. PTO and paid sick-leave pay treatment need an explicit employer policy. No medical diagnosis should be entered in request text.
9. Reimbursement approvals require receipt evidence and verified tax treatment. An approved expense is scheduled once for the next qualifying open period; it is not treated as an indefinite recurring reimbursement.
10. A typed name and explicit checkbox records acknowledgment of the exact stored wage/handbook terms. It does not replace the separate official tax-form or I-9 signature requirements.
11. Employee portal sessions last 30 days; invitations are single-use and expire after seven days. Workplace number defaults to 1 on sign-in and is shown in the employee portal.
12. QuickBooks defaults to sandbox unless explicitly configured for production. Accounting sync posts only finalized payroll. Automatic sync requires the admin to enable it after mapping verification.
13. Native tax calculation initially supports 2026 Maryland-resident, semimonthly employees with a verified 3.20% local rate. Other rates/states, nonresident and IRS lock-in cases, bonuses, and pretax deductions require separately verified calculations; unsupported years cannot be approved using 2026 FICA rules.
14. An overnight unpaid break without its actual timing is not allocated by guesswork. Admin resolves the time entries before approval.
15. Employer unemployment calculations assume a standard Maryland contributory employer and ordinary taxable employee wages. Admin must verify the assigned Maryland rate and FUTA credit treatment; no rate is silently chosen. Reimbursable employers, successor employers, exempt wages, and pretax-benefit tax treatment need additional support.
16. Payroll payment and government filing confirmations must reflect actual provider/bank/agency actions. Local test confirmations never represent real payments or filings.

17. Future hourly pay changes may take effect midweek and are appended after existing scheduled changes. Mixed workweeks require the server-verified weighted calculation described below. Decreases require documented advance written notice: 16 calendar days for semimonthly payroll (7 weekly, 14 biweekly, 31 monthly). This is a conservative operating rule, not a claim that every pay period is exactly that length.
18. Existing profiles supply an explicitly labeled opening rate at migration; unknown legacy rate history is not reconstructed. New hires get a hiring-date opening rate. Historical corrections require verified source compensation records.

19. Payroll is processed in chronological payment order within a tax year. Changing the payment date requires a fresh draft and approval; earlier payments cannot be inserted behind later approved/finalized payroll without reviewing its year-to-date impact. Payments cannot be confirmed as paid before their actual date. The isolated test harness injects a fixed clock solely to exercise historical synthetic payment fixtures.

20. Tax reconciliation covers finalized internal runs. Historical payments require separate detailed tax review. Quarterly deposit balances are accounting comparisons. The separate verified Form 941 calendar calculates federal deposit dates; other agencies still require separate deadline review. The filing comparison checks reported gross wages and tax control totals; matching totals do not validate every return box or prove agency acceptance without a real receipt.
21. Tax deposits are allocated to the agency and tax quarter on their receipt. Correcting a recorded deposit retains its void history; a later recorded filing for the same form and period supersedes the earlier comparison while preserving both records. Recording receipts does not move funds or transmit government forms.

22. Employer compliance starts with eight reviews: identity/EIN, Maryland withholding, unemployment, workers’ compensation, federal deposit/filing access, pay policies, leave policies, and recordkeeping/access. Reviews have a 90-day administrative reminder; this is not a statutory deadline. Applicable exceptions require evidence notes; employer identity, pay policies, and recordkeeping reviews cannot be waived.

23. A failed or cancelled QuickBooks authorization requires a fresh link. Local disconnect cancels pending and in-flight authorization from restoring access. Reconnect preserves mappings only for the same company and environment; remote Intuit application revocation is separate from deleting local access.

24. Rejecting a time entry preserves it for review but removes it from active clock status. It never creates replacement paid hours; the employee must clock a new shift or submit a correction for review.

25. A future pay change can be cancelled only while it is the latest active scheduled rate, before its effective date and before overlapping payroll is approved. Cancellation retains the original notice and requires a separately delivered cancellation notice. If the preceding rate is lower, the same conservative advance-notice interval as a decrease applies. A replacement is a new record with a fresh notice; cancelled records never supply worked-time or paid-leave rates.

26. Federal deposit scheduling currently covers the verified 2026 Form 941 monthly/semiweekly rules, DC legal holidays, quarter boundaries, and the $100,000 next-day rule with subsequent semiweekly scheduling. Admin verifies lookback/IRS records, prior-year next-day status, and complete daily tax history. Historical payments without daily tax detail keep the calendar in review status. Small-liability return-payment exceptions and deposit shortfall tolerances are not used to defer deadlines. Other tax years, state deadlines, special credit adjustments and agency relief remain separate work. FUTA carryforward and payment deadlines are implemented separately below the Form 941 calendar.
27. Form 941 deposit receipts are allocated to the earliest obligation within their recorded tax quarter; excess receipts never offset another quarter. Covered/late-covered labels describe this internal comparison, not confirmed agency allocation. Actual provider submission cutoffs can precede the legal deadline.

28. FUTA uses annual Form 940 receipt matching, applying recorded payments to the oldest liabilities in the same tax year even when they originated in different quarters. Amounts of $500 or less carry until a later quarter or the year-end payment deadline. Early deposits reduce prior-quarter carry; already-required deposits retain their original due dates. Open-quarter/year-end projections can change as further payroll is finalized. Employer FUTA rate/credit verification and complete payroll history are required; separate credit-reduction or special-case adjustments are not invented.

29. Maryland unemployment uses the verified standard 2026 contributory-employer quarterly dates (April 30, July 31, November 2, and February 1, 2027). Admin confirms the first and last required reporting quarter, full wage history, and absence of an agency extension, payment plan or reimbursable-employer arrangement. Zero-tax quarters still require a report when included in that verified range. Payment and filing receipts clear separate statuses; payroll outside the verified range requires review. Other-year deadlines and special arrangements remain separate work.

30. Marking an employee terminated takes effect immediately for new work: future scheduled shifts are cancelled and audited, new clocks and shift reactivation are blocked, and obsolete onboarding alerts close. Existing open clocks and historical shifts remain available for admin review. Former employees keep pay-record access and can acknowledge original or cancelled pay notices without waiving wage rights.

31. Maryland withholding uses the employer-verified 2026 monthly, quarterly, annual or approved seasonal schedule and required reporting periods. Annual MW506 and MW508 use January 31 (February 1, 2027 after the weekend), following COMAR and current agency guidance despite an inconsistent table in the 2026 guide. Zero-tax MW506 returns remain due. Receipts match oldest liabilities within the recorded quarter, or across the year for annual filers; matching is an internal reconciliation, not agency allocation confirmation. Accelerated accounts remain explicitly in review until their three-business-day and monthly requirements are automated.

32. Mixed-rate hourly workweeks use a weighted premium only when the server verifies the full observed workweek, closed calendar week, approved time and reconciled prior premiums. The target includes overtime earned through the current period; prior premiums are subtracted once. Unresolved history and overpayments require review. Ordinary workweeks retain their current calculation; only applied weighted weeks receive additional dependency locks. This does not enable salary, bonus regular-rate allocation or retroactive recovery.

## Server configuration

- `PAYROLL_DOCUMENT_KEY`: 64 hexadecimal characters representing a securely generated 32-byte encryption key. Provision through the deployment secret store. Back up and rotate using a managed procedure; replacing the key without re-encrypting stored records makes old documents and QuickBooks tokens unreadable. Never commit this key.
- `QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_ID`, `QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_SECRET`: Intuit application credentials.
- `QUICKBOOKS_REDIRECT_URI`: the backend's HTTPS `/api/payroll/quickbooks/callback` URL, registered exactly in Intuit.
- `QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT`: `sandbox` or `production`.
- Existing SMTP settings support invitations. No real invitations were sent during implementation validation.

## Verification

Use a dedicated localhost PostgreSQL instance, never the production database:

```sh
PAYROLL_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://payroll_test@127.0.0.1:55439/postgres node --test backend/payroll/__tests__/*.test.js
```

Each integration test creates and removes its own database schema. The harness refuses non-localhost database URLs and does not load application environment files.

Browser verification uses the actual payroll components and actual isolated HTTP/database routes:

```sh
PAYROLL_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://payroll_test@127.0.0.1:55439/postgres PAYROLL_TEST_PORT=4319 node backend/payroll/testing/serve.js
VITE_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4319 npm run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4173
PAYROLL_BROWSER_TEST=1 PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4173 npx playwright test tests/e2e/payroll-workforce.spec.ts --workers=1
```

Latest local verification: 46 payroll backend tests passed, including PostgreSQL onboarding/payroll/QuickBooks and compensation-history flows. The full browser flow passed with a future pay change, employee notice acknowledgment, and off-schedule payment date. TypeScript/build, scoped payroll lint, management smoke (12 checks), and launch smoke (10 checks) passed. A statement with two rates was rendered and visually inspected as a clean single-page PDF.

The browser harness is under `tests/support`; it is not included in the production entry points. Browser screenshots are captured under `/tmp` during verification. Live Intuit authorization and live bank/tax processing have not been verified.

Six weighted-overtime tests pass, covering partial prior payment, fully settled premium, overpayment, duplicate run references and workweek closure. This helper still needs authoritative finalized-run history loading and payroll/statement integration before mixed-rate approval can be enabled.

Frozen workweek payment records: each new preview now allocates actual rate-group pay into workweek straight-time earnings and overtime premiums without changing the period total. Deterministic largest-remainder allocation preserves rounding cents. Approval fingerprints include these records and finalization copies versioned workweek payments into the frozen employee statement snapshot. This establishes authoritative paid-premium evidence for later settlement; old statements are not retroactively assigned invented premiums. All 55 backend tests pass, including allocation invariance/rounding and verification that frozen weekly pay sums to finalized regular plus overtime pay. Mixed-rate payment enablement and history loading remain unfinished.

Authoritative workweek history integration: payroll previews now load prior finalized workweek payment records scoped to employee/facility and earlier reporting periods. The loader verifies exact whole-period hour and money totals, rejects duplicate/invalid weekly records, excludes unfinalized/current-period runs, and flags legacy or unreconciled evidence. Preview history verification also compares paid hours to carried prior-period time. Canonical fingerprints include this history. All 56 backend tests pass, including finalized snapshot reconciliation, employer isolation, unfinalized exclusions and missing/malformed evidence. Settlement calculation still needs to be applied to payable amounts and statements before mixed-rate payroll can be enabled.

Following-workweek context: preview loading now reads up to six days beyond the pay-period end while explicitly distinguishing current, prior and following entries. Only same-workweek following entries are retained for the employee's settlement context, with approval/open/break-ambiguity status. They are not added to current-period pay or prior-period overtime counters. The existing 56-test backend suite passes; a new targeted PostgreSQL test also passes for unverified following hours, unrelated-week exclusion and unchanged current pay. Following context is not yet used to approve weighted payments; integration must require complete verified context and include those dependencies in payment revalidation before enabling mixed rates.

Period-aware settlement review: the weighted rate now uses the entire observed workweek while the premium target is limited to overtime earned through the current pay period. Prior finalized premiums are subtracted once. Payroll previews calculate this review from prior earnings, current entries, following entries and verified paid history; open weeks, unapproved following time and missing history remain review states. Results explicitly say they are not applied to payroll amounts. All 59 backend tests pass, including a split-period premium whose two payments sum exactly to the full-week obligation and a full preview with unverified following hours. Pay calculation, statement display and time-dependency protection still need completion before mixed-rate approval is enabled.

Weighted payment/statement integration: verified settlements can now be applied inside the payroll engine. Their exact premiums are apportioned among overtime rate lines while preserving straight-time earnings, weekly payment records and gross totals; taxes use the revised gross. Invalid/open/duplicate settlements remain blocking. Statements show base hourly earnings plus the weighted premium instead of claiming a flat 1.5-times rate. All 62 backend tests pass, including different rates receiving overtime, exact rate/week reconciliation, engine gross/FICA and statement line amounts. A synthetic weighted statement was rendered and visually inspected as a clean single-page PDF.

The admin API does not yet activate this calculation path. Before activation, whole-workweek time dependencies must be protected after approval/finalization, settlement inputs must be revalidated and supplied by the server, and midweek rate changes must be exposed with the existing notice rules. This remains unfinished end-to-end functionality.

Weighted workweek time protection: the migration's time guard now protects every frozen workweek for an employee whose approved/finalized snapshot applies weighted overtime. Protection covers preceding/following days beyond the pay period, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and open timestamps. Other employees and unrelated weeks retain their normal behavior; voiding the run releases the added dependency lock. A direct concurrent insert waiting on the employer lock correctly sees approval after commit and is rejected. All 63 backend tests pass, including migration startup and the new lock/concurrency regression. Weighted admin activation, compensation dependency protection and revalidation remain unfinished.

Compensation dependency protection: rate scheduling and future-rate cancellation now share a check covering both ordinary approved/finalized pay periods and the affected employee's complete weighted workweeks. A change after the pay-period end but within the frozen workweek is rejected; unrelated employees, later weeks and voided runs are not blocked by this additional dependency check. All 63 backend tests pass, including these cases and existing compensation API workflows. The mutation routes retain employer-row locking before this check. Weighted API activation and full dependency fingerprints remain the next integration work.

Weighted server activation: payroll previews and drafts now apply server-derived settlements to mixed-rate workweeks, recalculate gross/taxes, retain applied settlement metadata and ignore client-supplied settlement amounts. Unresolved mixed weeks block approval. Applied following-period time is included in canonical approval/finalization comparisons. Locks now use per-workweek application markers, preserving unrelated ordinary weeks. The existing 63-test suite passes, and new API plus focused lock regressions pass for exact weighted gross, frozen draft premiums, client-input rejection and selective application. Complete weighted approval/finalization/browser verification and future midweek rate-entry UX remain outstanding.

Weighted approval/finalization verification: the real API now passes draft creation, native tax setup, review, approval and finalization with weighted rates. Frozen statement rate lines and weekly premiums reconcile to the paid total, and subsequent paid-time edits are rejected. Future midweek hourly rate changes are accepted through the admin endpoint while advance-notice and dependency checks remain enforced; the UI explains this behavior. All 64 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. A weighted browser workflow and follow-through on historical/cross-period correction cases remain required before declaring broader compensation work complete.

Weighted payroll review UI: calculation previews and saved run snapshots now show employee identity, workweek hours, the weighted hourly rate, overtime through the period, earned premiums, previously paid premiums and the amount applied. Unresolved weeks display their reason, corrective guidance and “Not applied”; prior run references are retained when available. The rate display is explicitly rounded while calculation remains exact. A new browser workflow uses an isolated real payroll API/database, verifies the $23 weighted rate and $92 premium in preview and saved review, then changes a time entry to unverified and verifies the blocked review state. The 390-pixel mobile card was visually inspected. That browser test, 12 focused engine tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Cross-period finalization/corrections and the broader outstanding requirement audit remain active work; this is not completion of the overall goal.

Cross-period weighted finalization verification: a closed 56-hour workweek spanning August 1–15 and August 16–31 now passes both actual API approvals and finalizations. The first run pays an $83.43 premium and the second uses its frozen payment evidence to pay the remaining $83.43; combined gross is $1,334.86 and combined premium $166.86, with exactly 56 paid hours. Changing following-period hours invalidates the first approval comparison; restoring them permits approval, which then prevents further changes even outside the first pay period. All 65 backend tests pass. This verifies normal consecutive-period settlement; retroactive corrections and off-cycle settlement remain outstanding. The current requirement matrix above has been updated to distinguish implemented weighted payroll from those remaining gaps.

Accelerated Maryland filing groundwork: MD MW506M is now a distinct accepted filing type in the admin receipt form, API reconciliation and database constraint. Receipts reconcile against finalized payroll by actual payment date for the recorded interval; replacements preserve superseded evidence, mismatches remain visible, and filing evidence never creates payment evidence. Tests cover confirmation requirements, facility isolation, duplicate references, mismatch/correction status and audit records. All 66 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Automated accelerated deadlines remain unfinished; recording MW506M does not itself implement or transmit accelerated returns.

Current accelerated-rule source verification: [Maryland Tax-General §10-822](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtg&section=10-822&enactments=false) requires qualifying filers to submit within three business days after payroll reaches $700 accumulated withholding and to file at least once each month. [The 2026 employer guide](https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/instructions/withholding/2026/withholding-guide.pdf) identifies MW506M and the $15,000 prior-year category threshold. Remaining calendar integration must account for accumulation, monthly reporting, prior filing/payment allocations, holidays and account waivers without treating a receipt as transmission.

Accelerated calendar implementation: the 2026 Maryland withholding calendar now groups finalized wages by actual pay date, creates a return/payment window at each $700 accumulation, and advances three business days excluding state holidays. Remaining monthly withholding and zero-return months receive separate monthly windows; an already-triggered month without remaining wages/withholding does not create an extra zero return. MW506M filing evidence and payment evidence remain independent. Existing automation consumes these deadlines. Different recorded accelerated-return intervals explicitly require allocation review instead of being treated as reconciled. Full backend suite passes 68 tests; focused follow-up tests also verify reminder dismissal for matching accelerated zero returns and reopening for an early return with a different interval. TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Browser verification and further early-return/account-allocation cases remain outstanding.

Assumption 33: accelerated filing is enabled only from the employer's verified account category and reporting months. The standard monthly residual/zero-return date uses the next month's 15th, adjusted for weekends/state holidays; threshold dates use three business days after the triggering pay date. This combines the Comptroller's monthly calendar with its accelerated pay-date rule. Voluntary early returns, waivers and special arrangements require account reconciliation and must not silently change allocation. References: [official withholding application guidance](https://interactive.marylandtaxes.gov/Business/bFile/Help/WITH_GenInfo_f.asp), [current COMAR withholding regulation](https://regs.maryland.gov/us/md/exec/comar/03.04.01.01), and [Comptroller filing calendar](https://services.marylandcomptroller.gov/taxes/en/business-reporting-requirements-other-assessments?id=kb_article_view&sysparm_article=KB0010164). The older application guidance is used for its explanation of pay-date accumulation, not as evidence that bFile remains the current filing portal.

Accelerated calendar browser verification: a new isolated real-API workflow configures accelerated reporting, displays the July 2 $700 threshold due July 8, records its accepted MW506M and confirms payment remains overdue, then records a July 9 payment and confirms COVERED LATE while the return remains RECORDED. Calendar items now offer Prepare return comparison, filling the exact form, dates, wages and tax totals while clearing old receipt/acceptance fields. The browser verifies those values before completing the receipt workflow. The mobile card was visually inspected at 390 pixels; TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Existing accelerated account-allocation review limitations and broader payroll gaps remain in the requirement audit.

Local filing receipt corrections: admins can now void an incorrectly entered tax filing receipt with a reason and explicit confirmation that only the local record is affected. The original receipt, payroll comparison and audit evidence remain; voided receipts no longer suppress filing reminders or supersede earlier valid records. Both Maryland calendars ignore voided receipts, including the accelerated interval-mismatch check. The real browser workflow verifies a recorded accelerated return becomes overdue again after correction while its payment remains COVERED LATE. API tests cover facility isolation, required confirmation, repeat-void rejection, predecessor restoration and audit records. All 68 backend tests, the expanded accelerated browser workflow, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass.

Assumption 34: receipt correction is local bookkeeping only. An agency-accepted return must still be amended or corrected through the agency/provider; the UI explains this before an admin voids the local evidence. Voided references remain reserved in the audit trail, and replacement evidence requires its own recorded reference.

Employee payroll reconciliation export: Reports now offers one row per paid employee for the selected actual-payment-date range, including former employees. It includes regular/overtime/other taxable wages, withholding components, reimbursements, deductions, net, employer FICA/FUTA/UI and finalized run references. Imported gross/tax/net remain separate with a review status; missing finalized tax components are flagged. The single database query preserves consistent aggregation, decimal formatting uses integer cents, exports are facility-scoped, audited and marked no-store, and CSV formula protection is retained. Tests verify year-boundary actual dates, draft exclusion, former employees, separate imported totals, facility boundaries, invalid dates, formula protection and export audit. All 69 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Browser download verification and detailed year-end tax forms remain outstanding.

Assumption 35: the employee summary is a payroll reconciliation report. Its wage/tax columns do not claim to calculate W-2 boxes or transmit year-end filings. Imported payments remain separately visible until their detailed tax components are reconciled. Default report dates cover the current calendar year; admins can select another range.

Employee summary browser verification: the real admin browser workflow now downloads a July employee reconciliation CSV, checks the requested date range and filename, validates the employee identity, $10,000 finalized gross and $700 Maryland withholding, and confirms incomplete finalized tax records are explicitly flagged. Reversed report dates disable download. The expanded workflow passes and the current production build passes. Existing large-bundle warnings remain; prerender is intentionally disabled. Detailed W-2/agency returns, correction payroll, broader pay configurations and live provider/deployment verification remain unfinished requirements.

Additional withholding frequencies: native 2026 withholding now accepts weekly, biweekly and monthly payroll frequencies alongside semimonthly for the existing Maryland-resident/3.20% local jurisdiction scope. Federal annualization uses 52/26/12 periods; Maryland uses the exact published brackets, deductions, exemptions and minimum gross thresholds for each frequency (2026 guide printed pages 37–38). An independent $4,000 monthly example exposed a floating-point half-cent error; Maryland now calculates bracket amounts with integer cents and basis-point arithmetic, with a v2 method identifier. Tests cover independent federal/state examples, published upper brackets, minimum wages, additional withholding and unsupported inputs. All 70 backend tests pass, plus the strengthened focused tax assertions and whitespace checks. Employer frequency settings, compatible generated calendars, leave accrual and complete browser/API payroll proof remain required before claiming end-to-end weekly/biweekly/monthly support.

Frequency calendar generation: a shared generator now supports weekly and biweekly schedules anchored to an explicit period start, plus monthly periods with a configured calendar-day payment lag. The admin generation endpoint uses the employer frequency instead of always creating semimonthly periods. Missing anchor/lag returns a configuration error; repeated generation returns existing periods. Pay dates retain the Federal Reserve bank-day rule and reject adjustments that would pay on/before the completed period's end. Tests cover year/month continuity, leap years, bank holidays, nominal payment-month selection, invalid configuration, API generation, idempotence and facility isolation. The full suite passes 75 tests; the subsequent bank-adjusted lag guard passes focused date tests. Settings UI/save validation, frequency-change overlap protections, automation integration, leave accrual and full payroll/browser verification remain outstanding before these frequencies are operationally complete.

Schedule overlap protection: manual generation now checks existing periods under the employer transaction lock and rejects conflicting ranges or a different frequency for the same range. The entire generation rolls back on conflict. Retained voided periods also require explicit transition handling, preventing the existing uniqueness rule from silently reusing an old record with the wrong frequency. Tests verify biweekly-to-weekly conflict rejection, unchanged row counts/frequencies and retained voided-period protection. The full suite passes 75 tests; the strengthened voided-period case passes focused integration tests. Automated generation still uses its existing semimonthly path; shared transactional persistence and a complete schedule-transition/settings UI remain the next integration work.

Shared calendar persistence and automation: manual and automated period creation now use the same overlap checks. Automation locks and reloads employer settings, derives the current month in the employer timezone, and creates the next three months atomically for every supported configured frequency. Existing payment-date overrides remain intact. Missing/invalid configuration or conflicting periods roll back generation and open a recoverable configuration alert while other workforce automation continues; valid regeneration dismisses that alert. Generation records an audit event only when periods are added. The full suite passes 76 tests, and subsequent focused tests verify the audit event is not duplicated on retry. Frequency settings/transition UI, leave-accrual adjustments and end-to-end non-semimonthly payroll remain outstanding.

Weekly/biweekly leave eligibility: Maryland sick accrual now applies the 24-hour biweekly threshold and the weekly combined current-plus-immediately-preceding-period threshold, alongside the existing 26-hour semimonthly rule. Weekly previews use the exact preceding finalized weekly payroll's worked minutes; first-hire periods may use zero preceding hours, and incomplete history requiring review blocks approval. Zero worked hours do not require prior history. Weighted preview rebuilding preserves these accrual results and blockers. Unit tests cover thresholds, current-period-only accrual and missing history; a real API test verifies missing-history blocking and 24 accrued minutes after verifying two 12-hour periods. The full suite passes 78 tests; focused engine tests pass after the zero-hours handling. Source: Maryland Department of Labor's earned sick/safe leave FAQ. Frequency setup/transition UX and complete non-semimonthly payroll verification remain outstanding.

Initial schedule setup UI/API: Employer setup now includes weekly, biweekly and semimonthly schedule selection, an anchor date/payment lag where applicable, and a three-month preview. Saving requires the published schedule reference and confirmation, replaces unused generated periods transactionally, and records before/after schedule evidence. Existing payroll runs or assigned reimbursements block this initial-replacement path and require a future dated transition. The payroll calendar now displays its configured frequency. API tests cover read-only preview, confirmation, replacement, audit records and used-payroll preservation. All 79 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Browser setup verification, existing-employer transitions and complete non-semimonthly payroll proof remain outstanding. Monthly calculation/generation helpers remain available internally, but monthly is not offered as ordinary Maryland hourly schedule setup because monthly eligibility needs a separately verified legal classification.

Schedule setup browser verification: a new isolated real-API browser workflow previews a biweekly schedule without creating periods, saves after entering the policy reference and confirmation, then reloads and verifies the saved frequency, anchor and payment lag. The dashboard settings response now includes the saved anchor/lag so the form no longer resets these to blank/default values. The mobile setup card was visually inspected at 390 pixels. Browser workflow, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Complete weekly/biweekly payroll finalization and dated transitions for employers with existing payroll remain outstanding.

Weekly/biweekly finalization proof: real API workflows now configure each frequency, generate its pay period, verify native tax elections, calculate worked time, create/review/approve/finalize payroll, and inspect frozen statements and posted leave. The weekly $1,000 example pays $776.01 net and posts 80 leave minutes; the biweekly $2,000 example pays $1,552.03 net and posts 160 leave minutes. Tax-election validation, returned method version and audit version now use the employer frequency instead of a hardcoded semimonthly value; the UI describes supported frequencies accurately. All 81 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. Full browser hire-to-pay coverage for these frequencies and dated schedule transitions remain outstanding, alongside the broader requirement audit gaps.

Period frequency preservation: payroll previews now use the selected period's recorded frequency for withholding and sick leave, rather than the employer's mutable current setting. Employee calculation snapshots retain that frequency and approval/finalization comparisons include it. Real API weekly and biweekly tests change the employer setting after draft creation and prove the existing period retains its tax/leave amounts and can be approved/finalized correctly. All 81 backend tests and whitespace checks pass. This removes a prerequisite risk for future dated schedule transitions; it does not itself implement that transition workflow.

Effective-dated calendar foundation: schedule versions now have a dedicated employer-scoped table, and both manual and automatic generation load that history. Periods use the schedule effective at their start; a cutover splitting the preceding period, an unaligned new anchor, duplicate effective dates or overlapping generated periods is rejected. Employers without versions retain the existing generator path. Initial setup cannot overwrite versioned history. Tests verify semimonthly-to-weekly date selection across the transition, historical preservation, mid-period rejection and gap prevention. All 82 backend tests and whitespace checks pass. This foundation does not yet provide the admin transition preview/save workflow or replacement of unused future periods; those remain active work.

Dated pay-schedule transition workflow: admins can now preview a future weekly, biweekly or semimonthly cutover and save it with a published employee-notice reference. The API requires a matching preview fingerprint, serializes on employer settings, preserves prior periods and runs, and replaces only unused OPEN future periods. Any future payroll run, assigned reimbursement, locked status, split boundary, unaligned anchor or existing pending transition blocks replacement. Version history preserves the original schedule and subsequent automatic/manual generation selects the correct period-start version. The preview retains the preceding period's actual saved payment date, including overrides. Dashboard frequency, tax-election methods and current compensation metadata resolve the effective schedule for today. Saved history is visible after reload. All 84 backend tests passed; the two schedule browser workflows, TypeScript, scoped lint and mobile visual inspection passed. Focused effective-date and reimbursement-protection assertions also passed after the final preview correction.

36. Schedule transitions use complete existing period boundaries, with the effective date as the new weekly/biweekly anchor. Administrators verify published employee notice before saving. One future transition is allowed at a time; replacing periods with payroll or assigned expenses is refused to preserve their references. Cancelling/replacing a pending transition, employee-side schedule acknowledgments, explicit delivery-date/notice-rule validation, and weekly leave eligibility across a frequency transition remain active follow-up work. The UI does not transmit notices itself.

Pending schedule correction completed: the history panel now previews and cancels the latest future schedule transition, with cancellation notice confirmation and a delivery reference. Cancellation restores the preceding schedule for unused future periods, preserves earlier payroll and records the original version with cancellation metadata. Active-version queries exclude cancelled versions, and a partial unique index permits a corrected replacement on the same effective date while retaining prior records. Both save paths require a current preview fingerprint. Real API tests cover restoration, same-date replacement, stale preview rejection, future-run protection and complete rollback on an audit-write failure. The real browser workflow cancels through the UI and verifies the retained record after reload; its mobile layout was inspected. All 84 backend tests, both schedule browser workflows, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks passed. The focused rollback/protection additions also pass. Assumption 36's pending-transition cancellation gap is now resolved; employee acknowledgments, notice-date validation and leave eligibility across frequency transitions remain active work.

Payday notice-date enforcement: Maryland Labor and Employment §3-504(a)(3) requires at least one pay period's advance notice of a payday change (official source checked: https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gle&section=3-504&enactments=false). Transition and cancellation saves now require a valid actual notice-delivery date, never future-dated, and persist it in version history and audit records. Previews return the notice deadline and the admin history displays delivered dates. The transition deadline is the start of the complete preceding period, a conservative implementation relative to the changed payday. For cancellation, the deadline also allows at least the announced schedule's period length (7/14/16/31 days); cancellation delivery cannot precede original delivery. This conservative policy is an implementation assumption, not a claim that the statute defines those exact day counts. Tests cover invalid dates, future dates, late notice, stored dates, transition/cancellation workflows and retained history. All 85 backend tests and both browser workflows passed, along with TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks. Employee-side schedule notices and acknowledgments remain the next implementation step.

Employee schedule notice receipts: the employee Pay statements view now shows employer schedule change notices and their cancellations, with separate receipt acknowledgments. An acknowledgment preserves the schedule notice snapshot, uses the authenticated employee identity, and is idempotent; repeats do not duplicate receipts or audit events. Cancelled changes cannot receive new change acknowledgments, while cancellation receipts remain available to former employees. Admin schedule history exposes per-employee change/cancellation receipt status, including unacknowledged records. Receipt acknowledgment is separate from advance notice delivery and does not waive wage rights. Employer/internal delivery references are omitted from the employee payload. Admin and employee routes are registered separately, and the explicit authenticated employee route allowlist includes the two new endpoints. Real API coverage checks scoping, invalid confirmation, repeat requests, cancellation state and former-employee access. The new browser test redeems an invitation, acknowledges both notices, and verifies both receipts in the admin view; its mobile notice card was visually inspected. TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. This closes the employee schedule acknowledgment gap; weekly leave across frequency changes and the broader requirement audit remain active work.

Weekly leave at a frequency transition: the first weekly period can now use the immediately preceding finalized semimonthly or biweekly period's worked minutes when active schedule history records that exact cutover. Prior period boundaries must match the prior frequency; undocumented or cancelled transitions do not enable the fallback. Hours from the prior period establish eligibility only, and accrual remains based on current-period work. The prior period, frequency, run and worked minutes are preserved in calculation fingerprints, saved drafts and finalized statement snapshots, with an admin review panel explaining the basis. Tests verify both prior frequencies, 12+12-hour eligibility producing 24 new leave minutes, below-threshold nonaccrual, undocumented history and cancelled transitions. All 88 backend tests pass; the real browser workflow verifies preview and saved-draft evidence. TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass.

37. For the first weekly period after a documented frequency change, “immediately preceding pay period” means the full prior pay period, including when it used a different frequency. This follows the wording in Maryland's official sick-leave FAQ (https://www.labor.md.gov/paidleave/paidleavefaqs.shtml), but the FAQ does not expressly describe frequency transitions. This interpretation can be more generous than limiting prior hours to seven days. Only finalized prior hours are accepted automatically; incomplete prior payroll remains a review blocker when current hours alone do not establish eligibility. No prior hours accrue leave twice.

Accumulated sick-leave cap: payroll accrual now checks both the 40-hour annual allowance and the 64-hour accumulated balance limit. Ledger balance is computed as of the payroll payment date, so later-dated leave bookings do not create premature room under the cap. Existing balances above the limit receive no additional payroll accrual and are not reduced by this calculation. Balance and annual accrual before payroll are included in approval fingerprints and frozen statement evidence, and the admin review panel now shows those values for every payroll frequency. Tests cover near-cap, at-cap, above-cap, annual-limit interaction, used leave and future bookings. All 90 backend tests pass, along with TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks. This corrects the missing accumulated-balance limit; fractional accrual preservation and annual rollover remain outstanding. Source for the 64-hour minimum-policy cap: https://www.labor.md.gov/paidleave/paidleavefaqs.shtml and https://www.labor.maryland.gov/paidleave/paidleaveposter.shtml, checked during the preceding leave review.

Fractional sick-leave preservation: accrual now carries an integer remainder measured in thirtieths of one leave minute, rather than flooring each period independently. Eligible periods combine current work with the prior finalized remainder; ineligible periods preserve the remainder. When an annual or accumulated balance limit is reached, excess accrual and its remainder are not banked beyond that limit. Fraction state is shown in payroll review, saved in drafts, included in approval fingerprints using explicit fields (avoiding PostgreSQL JSON key-order differences), and frozen on finalized statements. The next run reads the most recent finalized fraction. Older runs with positively accrued leave and identifiable untracked fractional work block with LEAVE_FRACTION_HISTORY_REQUIRED; internal reconciliation for that historical case remains outstanding. Legacy records whose eligible worked time is an exact multiple of 30 minutes can establish a zero remainder. Tests verify fractional combination, ineligible-period preservation, caps, invalid remainders, legacy review, real draft persistence and real API finalization snapshot fields. All 92 backend tests pass, as do the browser preview/saved-draft workflow, TypeScript, scoped lint, whitespace checks and mobile inspection. Annual rollover is still outstanding.

Leave ledger classification: manual entries can now identify opening balances, restorations, frontloaded grants or ordinary earned/use adjustments. Opening balances and restorations increase available leave without consuming the current year's accrual allowance; frontloaded grants and positive ordinary adjustments count toward that allowance. Payroll-posted entries are explicitly PAYROLL_ACCRUAL, and existing entries with a payroll source are classified from that reliable linkage. Unclassified historical manual entries retain their previous treatment rather than guessing from their reason text. Special positive grants require a detailed source reference. Real API tests verify opening/restored balances, annual-allowance separation and frontload treatment. All 92 backend tests pass, including payroll finalization; TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. The browser workflow records an opening balance through Pay setup & leave and verifies its stored classification; the mobile form was inspected. This is groundwork for annual rollover and imported-balance reconciliation, not completion of those workflows.

Annual leave opening workflow: Pay setup & leave now previews and applies a calendar-year opening with a verified published-policy reference. Accrual policies carry up to the selected 40–64 hour limit; frontloaded policies replace unused balances with the selected 40–64 hour annual grant. Former employees retain their recorded balance. The preview shows every reduction and grant and requires explicit policy confirmation. Earlier nonfinal payroll, approved/finalized new-year payroll, existing frontload/rollover entries, later closures, negative balances and insufficient balances for used/reserved new-year leave prevent application. A fingerprint catches changed balance/policy inputs. Application and its audit are transactional; a unique employer/year record prevents duplicate grants. Database guards preserve prior-year sick-leave entries and the opening adjustment/grant after closure; documented current-year corrections remain available. Tests verify carryover, frontload, duplicate prevention, employer scoping, audit-failure rollback, used payroll and reserved-leave protections. All 94 backend tests passed before the final reserved-leave guard; the focused annual-opening tests passed afterward. The browser preview/apply/duplicate workflow, TypeScript, scoped lint, whitespace checks and mobile inspection pass. Automatic recurring year opening, saved opening-history review and historical fraction reconciliation remain active work.

38. The default annual policy is a calendar year, 40-hour carryover for accrual employees, and a replacement 40-hour grant for frontloaded employees. Admins can select 40–64 hours and must verify this matches the published policy before applying any balance reduction. Exempt-review policies require resolution first. Former employees' balances are preserved for subsequent rehire handling. Closed-period corrections use dated current-year entries, preserving the original opening audit. These are explicit product assumptions; employers with other benefit years or more generous allowances need additional policy configuration.

Recurring annual leave opening and history: admins can save an explicitly verified future-year policy, enable or pause automatic opening, and inspect each prior opening's preserved employee adjustments and grants. Workforce automation processes the earliest eligible unopened year using the same locked, transactional application helper as manual opening. Retries cannot duplicate a year; unresolved payroll or leave conflicts create a dedicated critical alert, and successful recovery or disabling the policy dismisses it. The policy starts in a future year to avoid silently applying a retroactive balance reduction on configuration. Missed years are processed one per automation run in chronological order. Tests cover year boundaries, duplicate retries, frontload replacement, conflict alerts, recovery, pause/resume, history and employer scoping. All 95 backend tests pass; the additional pause/alert assertions also pass. The browser workflow saves the recurring policy, reloads it, and expands opening history. TypeScript, scoped lint, whitespace checks and mobile visual inspection pass. The application automation hook is integrated; no production deployment or real scheduled execution has been claimed. Historical fraction reconciliation and the broader hire-to-pay requirement audit remain active.

Historical leave-fraction reconciliation: Pay setup & leave now previews identifiable discarded fractions for the selected employee, shows the source finalized runs, and applies a verified recovery without rewriting paid statements. Whole recovered minutes post as a current-date RESTORATION, and a preserved checkpoint supplies the residual fraction to subsequent payroll. Preview fingerprints, an employee/run uniqueness constraint and transactional audit prevent stale or duplicate credits. Recovery starts after the latest tracked fraction/checkpoint and excludes rounded-up, partial and known cap-limited accrual. An administrator confirms that the candidate fractions were not already restored and verifies the historical policy. Unknown historical cap/policy context is not claimed to be reconstructed automatically. All 97 backend tests passed before the final cap-evidence refinement; focused recovery/carry tests passed after it. The browser preview/confirmation/apply/duplicate workflow, TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks pass. This resolves the internal recovery path for identifiable legacy rounding losses; unsupported or incomplete historical payroll still requires documented review.

39. Historical fraction recovery is an additional leave adjustment authorized after reviewing the original records and prior corrections. It uses runs whose stored accrual equals the whole-minute floor of eligible work and excludes known cap cases. When older snapshots omit cap or policy evidence, the admin must verify that context before applying the proposed credit. Credits are dated when reconciliation is applied and do not alter previous payroll statements or consume current-year earned-accrual allowance.

Salaried-hire onboarding foundation: People & onboarding now accepts hourly or salary pay. Salary hires require a positive annual amount, store no fabricated hourly rate or hourly pay-rate record, and enter EXEMPT_REVIEW classification status. Employee and admin views display annual compensation, and the acknowledged wage notice preserves the annual amount. Ordinary salary-employee profile updates no longer fail on a null hourly rate; attempts to change salary/pay basis through that generic profile endpoint are explicitly redirected to compensation review. Readiness checks require salary classification review. The API test covers creation, validation, packet readiness, ordinary edits, invitation redemption, employee-facing salary and signed terms. The browser test creates a $78,000 salary hire and verifies the employee portal display at mobile width. All 98 backend tests, TypeScript, scoped lint, whitespace checks and browser/mobile checks pass. Salary payroll calculation, duties/salary-basis review, dated salary changes, partial-period treatment and salaried nonexempt overtime remain active implementation work. No claim of payable salary support is made yet.

40. Selecting salary does not establish an overtime exemption. New salary hires require explicit classification review; role duties and salary basis must be verified before exempt calculation is enabled. Current federal guidance was checked at https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/17a-overtime and https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/17g-overtime-salary. State-specific requirements and special exemption categories must also be respected by the calculation workflow.

Salary classification review: Pay setup & leave now records exempt or nonexempt classification, the reviewed job title, evidence reference, actual-duties assessment, salary-basis verification and Maryland-rule verification. Standard exempt review checks the $35,568 annual threshold and a supported executive, administrative or professional category; salary amount or title never assigns exemption automatically. Pay-setup completion requires the review, and recording/replacing a review reopens that onboarding task. Classification and role changes are audited transactionally; a synthetic audit failure confirms both roll back. Approved or finalized employee payroll prevents replacement through this initial-review route. The general details form now omits hourly-rate inputs and submissions for salary hires, and hourly compensation scheduling is hidden for them. Browser verification covers hiring, exempt review, reload persistence, ordinary profile saving and employee annual-salary display. Mobile layout was inspected. All 100 backend tests passed; focused tests also passed after adding the audit-failure assertion. TypeScript, scoped lint, whitespace checks and production build passed (existing bundle-size warning remains). Salary calculation, dated salary/classification changes, partial-period rules and salaried nonexempt overtime are still unfinished; classification review alone does not enable payroll approval.

41. Initial salary classification supports standard Maryland executive, administrative and learned/creative professional exemptions with explicit evidence. The $684 weekly / $35,568 annual threshold was checked against Maryland guidance at https://www.labor.maryland.gov/labor/wagepay/wpsalaried.shtml and federal guidance at https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime/salary-levels. Special exemptions and other states need separate rules. The initial nonexempt salary setup assumes a fixed 40-hour workweek; calculation and a dated compensation-change path remain required before this supports actual salary payment.

Exempt salary calculation: reviewed standard Maryland exempt employees now receive fixed annual salary divided by 52, 26, 24 or 12 pay periods, rounded to integer cents. Current annual salary, title and work state must match the recorded exempt review. Salary bypasses hourly-rate and weighted-overtime earnings, retains actual recorded work minutes separately, and uses the existing tax and deduction pipeline. Paid leave is included in the salary amount; approval records its hours with an explicit included-in-salary flag and no fabricated hourly rate. The admin calculation preview and saved review show salary basis and leave assumptions. Finalized statement snapshots preserve salary calculation details; PDF statement lines show salary and annual compensation rather than zero-dollar hourly wages. Salary calculation is part of draft/approval fingerprints. Weekly leave history uses the finalized salary leave basis when present. Tests cover fixed amounts at all four frequencies, partial hiring, mismatched review, 48 recorded work hours without exempt overtime, paid-leave inclusion, weekly/biweekly real API calculation and finalization, taxes, leave accrual and saved statements. Browser salary-preview/draft-review verification and mobile inspection passed, as did TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks. Nonexempt salary calculation and dated changes remain unfinished.

42. Exempt salary is paid in full for each scheduled pay period overlapping employment, including an initial or final partial period. No absence deductions or automatic salary proration are applied. This is a deliberately more generous payment policy; federal salary-basis rules permit certain deductions but do not require them (https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/17g-overtime-salary). Weekly/biweekly salary uses 52/26 periods even in a calendar year containing an extra payday. A reviewed alternative policy and dated salary changes remain future work.

43. The current exempt salary leave basis is a regular Monday–Friday, eight-hour workday, totaling 40 hours per week. Only dates within employment count; holidays and paid leave preserve that assumed basis. Maryland assumes 40 weekly hours for exempt employees unless their normal workweek is shorter (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/laws/StatuteText?article=gle&enactments=false&section=3-1304). Shorter or alternate workweeks require additional configuration; the current assumption must be adjusted for those hires. Actual clock hours do not reduce or increase this exempt leave basis.

Nonexempt salary calculation: the initial salary agreement can now explicitly record a fixed 40-hour workweek and an admin-verified applicable minimum wage. Nonexempt salary pays the fixed period amount plus 1.5 times annual salary / 2,080 for approved overtime minutes, retaining fractional regular-rate precision until the final cent rounding. Existing weekly time allocation includes preceding-period hours, and nonexempt leave uses actual approved work instead of the exempt assumed-hours basis. Salary must cover 2,080 hours at the verified minimum wage before calculation or pay-setup completion. Paid leave stays included in the base salary. Statements and admin review separate salary from salary overtime. Additional bonus earnings currently block nonexempt salary approval until workweek allocation is implemented. Tests cover the salary formula, carried prior-week hours, minimum-wage and agreement guards, paid leave, weekly/biweekly finalization, tax outputs and statement details. Browser tests exercise both exempt and nonexempt calculations, including saving the nonexempt agreement through the UI; both passed, with mobile review inspected. TypeScript, scoped lint and whitespace checks passed. Dated salary changes, shorter fixed workweeks, bonus allocation, local minimum-wage automation and broader completion requirements remain active.

44. Nonexempt salary is a fixed 40-hour agreement, with annual salary converted to weekly salary using 52 weeks. Overtime is additional time-and-a-half after 40 actual worked hours, without averaging workweeks. This is not a fluctuating-workweek agreement. The regular-rate basis follows the U.S. DOL overtime guidance at https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/field-operations-handbook/Chapter-32 and https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/legacy/files/2006_06_01_10NA_FLSA.pdf. The same full-period/no-absence-deduction payment assumption applies to this salary configuration. Other salary agreements require additional configuration.

45. An admin verifies and records the highest applicable minimum wage for the salary employee's work locations; the UI starts at the $15 Maryland statewide floor but requires explicit verification. Local rates can be higher, as documented by Maryland at https://labor.maryland.gov/labor/wages/wagehrfacts.shtml. Automatic dated county/rate selection is not yet implemented. The verified amount is preserved in salary review and payroll calculation snapshots.
